finding.claim: deleteAccount never enforces its authorization check: canDelete(u, a) is evaluated but its boolean result is discarded, so any caller can delete any account by id.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled path parameter `long id` on DELETE /accounts/{id}, with any authenticated non-admin User u. Precondition: the target account exists and the attacker is not its owner.

trace.note: canDelete returns u.admin() || a.ownerId() == u.id(); the logic itself is correct.
deleteAccount(User u, long id) receives the caller and the attacker-chosen id.
a = accounts.get(id) loads the victim account with no ownership filter.
canDelete(u, a) is called as a bare statement; its boolean is dropped. No throw and no return guard, so execution always continues.
accounts.remove(id) runs unconditionally, deleting the account for any caller.

finding.guards_checked: (1) canDelete at line 10 is correct but unused on this path. (2) assertCanDelete at lines 13-17, the guard that throws SecurityException, is not called in deleteAccount; closeAccount at line 29 uses it correctly. (3) No other check exists in deleteAccount. (4) Caller authentication and the origin of User.admin are not in this repo, so I could not verify them. The bypass holds regardless, because the ownership check is absent even for an authenticated caller.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. canDelete (AccountService.java:9-11) is correct but its bool is discarded as a bare statement at line 22. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) is never called from deleteAccount; it is only used by closeAccount at line 29. No other check exists in deleteAccount (lines 20-24), and a directory grep finds no other callers or wrappers.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: canDelete's result is discarded at AccountService.java:22 and accounts.remove(id) runs unconditionally at line 23, so any caller who can invoke deleteAccount can delete an account they do not own (the attacker needs only a User object, and the authentication code that builds it is not in this repo).

finding.claim: Null account from a missing id causes a NullPointerException for non-admin callers in deleteAccount and closeAccount. The resulting error-vs-success difference lets a low-privilege user enumerate which account ids exist, and the unhandled exception may surface as a 500.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled `long id` on DELETE /accounts/{id} or POST /accounts/{id}/close, with a non-admin User. Precondition: the id does not exist in the map.
finding.sink: a.ownerId() at AccountService.java:10, reached via canDelete from line 22 or assertCanDelete at line 29 (existence oracle and unhandled error path).

trace.note: deleteAccount: accounts.get(id) returns null for a missing id; no null check.
canDelete(u, null): if u is not admin, the || short-circuit does not apply, so a.ownerId() is evaluated.
closeAccount has the same pattern: a is null for a missing id.
assertCanDelete calls canDelete, which dereferences null at line 10 for non-admins.

finding.guards_checked: No null check on the result of accounts.get at lines 21 or 28. Admins avoid the NPE because the short-circuit at line 10 returns true before dereferencing a. Severity is low: the oracle reveals only id existence, and the NPE does not change state because it fires before remove.

verdict.guard_found: none. canDelete (AccountService.java:9-11) has no null check, and deleteAccount (line 21-22) discards its boolean result as a bare statement. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) does not catch the NPE, and closeAccount (lines 28-29) calls it before accounts.remove. Admins short-circuit at line 10 and avoid the NPE.
verdict.reason: For a non-admin caller and a missing id, accounts.get returns null (AccountService.java:21 and :28), and canDelete dereferences a.ownerId() at line 10 before any check, so an NPE is thrown before remove runs. The NPE versus success/SecurityException difference is a real existence oracle for any authenticated low-privilege user, though the endpoint wiring is outside this repo and the 500 behavior is unverified. The candidate missed a worse issue in the same method: deleteAccount computes canDelete at line 22 and ignores the result, so any authenticated user can delete any existing account.
